t:
(a) 
The first sentence of section 9(a) of the Railroad Retirement Act of 1937 is amended by inserting after “individual”, where it appears the third time, the following: “or, on the basis of the same compensation, any other individual,”.
 
    (b) 
The second sentence of such section 9(a) is amended by striking out the phrase “such individual” where it first appears in such sentence, and inserting in lieu thereof “the individual to whom more than the correct amount has been paid”.

fable.w: This section only makes technical wording amendments to section 9(a) of the Railroad Retirement Act of 1937, which concerns recovering erroneous payments. Because the text mentions "individual" and overpayments, it could be mistaken for a provision giving outsiders a say, but it creates no comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation with non-federal parties, or right to sue. No party outside the federal government is brought into any federal decision.

qwen_block.w: This section amends the Railroad Retirement Act to clarify the definition of individuals liable for overpayments. It does not establish any mechanism for public participation, consultation, or advisory input. The changes are purely technical adjustments to statutory language regarding financial liability, not procedural requirements for outside involvement in federal decision-making.
qwen_block.s: The first sentence of section 9(a) of the Railroad Retirement Act of 1937 is amended by inserting after “individual”, where it appears the third time, the following: “or, on the basis of the same compensation, any other individual,”.
qwen_block.b: Temptation: The text mentions "individuals" and "compensation," which might suggest some form of interaction or benefit application. However, the text is purely technical, amending the definitions and references within a statute regarding overpayments. It does not describe a process where outsiders consult with the government, nor does it grant rights to sue or participate in decision-making. It is a legislative amendment to clarify who is liable for repayment of overpayments.

opus.w: This section only rewords section 9(a) of the Railroad Retirement Act of 1937 so that it refers to 'any other individual' paid on the same compensation, and to 'the individual to whom more than the correct amount has been paid.' No one outside the federal government is consulted or given a role in any federal decision. The link to railroad retirement benefits might look relevant, but benefit administration and overpayment adjustments are not participation under the definition.
opus.b: The one tempting reading is that this concerns a federal benefits program, but that doesn't hold up. Section 9(a) of the Railroad Retirement Act of 1937 deals with overpayments, and this text only changes the wording of that section. It sets up no consultation, comment period, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue, and benefit applications and payments don't count as participation anyway.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the Railroad Retirement Act to clarify the definition of individuals eligible for correction of overpayments. It does not require or recommend any form of participation such as public comment, consultation with outside entities, or advisory boards. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits, and this text pertains to the administrative correction of benefit payments rather than a participatory process in federal decision-making.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that amending the Railroad Retirement Act affects individuals (beneficiaries), and thus involves them. However, the definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants." This section merely clarifies the legal definition of who is eligible for a correction of overpayments; it does not establish a process for public comment, consultation, or advisory input from outside parties regarding a federal decision. The actors involved are the individuals receiving benefits and the agency administering them, but the mechanism is administrative correction, not participatory decision-making.
